events.title: Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence founded (later MIRI)
events.label: SIAI / MIRI founded
events.problem: Research specifically about beneficial superhuman AI had little institutional support. SIAI provided a small independent home for this line of work.
events.idea: Eliezer Yudkowsky, Brian Atkins and Sabine Atkins founded the Singularity Institute. Its early Friendly AI programme investigated how a more capable AI could retain goals beneficial to humans; the organisation later became MIRI.
events.changed: An early independent organisation concerned with superhuman AI that developed the Friendly AI agenda. Its writing and research helped form the community around later alignment work; it became MIRI in 2013.
events.limits: Its theoretical agenda (decision theory, agent foundations) had little influence on mainstream ML. Since about 2023 MIRI has said that alignment research is not on track, and it now works mainly on public communication and policy, arguing for a halt to frontier development.

links.note: mesa-optimization paper was written largely by MIRI-affiliated authors
same early community of x-risk thinkers

terms.def: The problem of making an AI system reliably pursue the goals its designers intend, including in situations they did not foresee.

verified.note: MIRI About page gives 2000 founding, founders and 2013 rename. Page returns 403 to curl but loaded via WebFetch.

events.date_context: Founding year reported by MIRI; an exact founding day is not asserted.

events.title: Future of Humanity Institute founded at Oxford
events.label: FHI founded
events.problem: Existential-risk and long-term AI questions were dispersed across disciplines. FHI aimed to provide an academic institution where they could be investigated together.
events.idea: Nick Bostrom founded the Future of Humanity Institute within Oxford's Faculty of Philosophy, initially as a 3-year project, to study big-picture questions about humanity's long-term future.
events.changed: Provided an influential academic home for existential-risk research, including Bostrom's Superintelligence and early AI-governance work. GovAI originated as an FHI programme before becoming independent.
events.limits: Its research ranged from philosophy and strategy to technical questions. The institute's retrospective attributes its closure to administrative constraints, including a 2020 hiring and fundraising freeze; that account is an institutional perspective.

terms.def: A risk that could cause human extinction or permanently and drastically curtail humanity's potential.

verified.note: FHI final site opened 6 Nov 2026: established in 2005, initially for three years; closed 16 April 2024. Unsupported November precision removed.

events.date_context: FHI's retrospective confirms 2005; the previously supplied month was not supported and is omitted.

events.title: DeepMind founded in London
events.label: DeepMind founded
events.problem: Building general AI was an ambitious research-company goal rather than a clearly established product category. DeepMind combined that goal with learning-based systems and game benchmarks.
events.idea: Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman founded DeepMind in London with the explicit mission to build general AI. Legg had written about AGI risk before founding it.
events.changed: Became a major AGI-focused lab, producing DQN and AlphaGo. Google acquired it in 2014; in April 2023 it merged with Google Brain to form Google DeepMind, whose later safety work includes the Frontier Safety Framework.
events.limits: An AGI mission and safety research do not establish that resulting systems are safe. Claims about an independent ethics-board condition in the Google acquisition are press-reported and should not be read as evidence of effective oversight.

sources.label: Google DeepMind: About (started 2010; merger with Google Brain)

links.note: AlphaGo made AGI timelines feel shorter for many
later safety framework from the same lab

terms.def: Artificial general intelligence: a system that can match or exceed humans across most cognitive tasks, not just one domain.

verified.note: DeepMind About page confirms 2010. Founders and 2014 acquisition from well-known secondary record; ethics-board condition is press-reported, not confirmed by Google.

events.date_context: Founding year, rather than a precise incorporation or announcement day.

events.title: Future of Life Institute founded; Puerto Rico conference (Jan 2015)
events.label: FLI founded
events.problem: AI-risk researchers wanted wider contact with mainstream ML researchers and a source of support for beneficial-AI research.
events.idea: Max Tegmark, Jaan Tallinn, Viktoriya Krakovna, Anthony Aguirre and Meia Chita-Tegmark founded FLI (launch event at MIT). In January 2015 it convened AI researchers in Puerto Rico, published an open letter on research priorities for robust and beneficial AI, and Elon Musk funded its first grant programme.
events.changed: Helped connect AI-risk discussions to mainstream researchers through convenings and a 2015 research-grant programme. It later organised the Asilomar Principles and the 2023 pause letter, and continued policy and advocacy work.
events.limits: Convenings, grants and open letters have different effects. The letters and principles were voluntary; signatures alone do not demonstrate changes in model development or deployment.

sources.label: FLI: Our history (founded May 2014; Puerto Rico 2–5 Jan 2015)

links.note: FLI was founded before the July 2014 book; its January 2015 Puerto Rico conference came later in the same wider AI-risk debate.

verified.note: FLI history page says founded May 2014 (other sources say March 2014; the page is the primary source) and gives the 2–5 Jan 2015 conference dates. The Musk grant is not on that page; it is well documented elsewhere but not re-checked here.

events.date_context: FLI's own history dates its founding to May 2014; the Puerto Rico conference was in January 2015.

events.title: OpenAI founded as a non-profit
events.label: OpenAI founded
events.problem: The founders argued that a leading AI research institution should prioritise broad public benefit as machine intelligence became more capable.
events.idea: Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others announced OpenAI as a non-profit research company, with over $1 billion pledged and a mission to make AGI benefit all of humanity.
events.changed: Grew into a major frontier lab that developed GPT models, large-scale RLHF and ChatGPT. Its changing corporate structure and the 2023 board crisis made it an important case for examining mission-driven governance under commercial pressure.
events.limits: The initial commitment to broadly sharing research changed as systems became more capable, including staged release of GPT-2. A public-benefit mission and a non-profit board do not by themselves establish effective oversight.

links.note: the non-profit board structure set up here was tested in 2023

verified.note: Opened the dated OpenAI primary announcement on 6 Nov 2026; confirms 2015-12-11.

events.title: Open Philanthropy makes AI risk a major funding priority
events.label: Open Phil prioritises AI risk
events.problem: Karnofsky argued that advanced-AI risk was important and neglected, and that long-term philanthropy could support more technically informed research and institution building.
events.idea: Holden Karnofsky announced that Open Philanthropy (funded mainly by Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna) would treat potential risks from advanced AI as a major priority, aiming to grow the number of technically strong people working on it.
events.changed: Became a major funder of AI-safety research, organisations and fellowships, including CHAI, OpenAI and later independent groups. It changed its name to Coefficient Giving on 18 November 2025.
events.limits: Concentrated funding from one donor gave a small network outsized influence on research agendas; critics also point to close personal ties between funders and grantee labs.

sources.label: Karnofsky: Potential Risks from Advanced AI – The Philanthropic Opportunity (6 May 2016)
Coefficient Giving: The story behind our new name (18 Nov 2025)

links.note: CHAI launched with a $5.5M Open Phil grant
Open Phil was Redwood's main funder

verified.note: Opened primary Coefficient Giving page, dated 6 May 2016, and the rename announcement dated 18 Nov 2025.

events.title: Center for Human-Compatible AI launched at UC Berkeley
events.label: CHAI launched
events.problem: Russell and collaborators wanted a sustained academic programme focused on AI systems that learn human preferences and remain beneficial as capabilities grow.
events.idea: UC Berkeley launched CHAI under Stuart Russell, with a $5.5M Open Philanthropy grant plus FLI and Leverhulme funding, to reorient AI toward 'provably beneficial' systems that are uncertain about human preferences and learn them (e.g. via inverse reinforcement learning).
events.changed: Created a sustained beneficial-AI research programme in a major ML department. Its students later worked across academia and frontier labs, and Russell's Human Compatible popularised the assistance-game framing.
events.limits: Its assistance-game formalism is elegant but has been hard to scale to LLM-era systems; most frontier alignment work took a more empirical route.

links.note: funded by Open Phil's new AI priority

terms.def: Inferring the reward function an agent is optimising from observations of its behaviour.

verified.note: Opened Berkeley News launch article: 29 Aug 2016; confirms $5.5M Open Phil grant and additional FLI/Leverhulme support.

events.title: Asilomar AI Principles
events.label: Asilomar AI Principles
events.problem: After the 2015 open letter there was still no shared, concrete statement of norms that AI researchers and industry leaders would sign.
events.idea: At FLI's Beneficial AI 2017 conference in Asilomar (early January 2017), participants agreed 23 principles covering research, ethics and values, and longer-term issues such as recursive self-improvement and avoiding an AGI arms race.
events.changed: One of the earliest widely signed AI governance texts, signed by leaders from DeepMind, OpenAI and academia. California's legislature endorsed it in 2018, and its language echoes in later lab principles and summit declarations.
events.limits: Entirely voluntary, with no mechanism for monitoring or enforcement; several principles (e.g. avoiding arms races) were plainly not followed in the years after.

verified.note: Conference dates per FLI history page (3–8 Jan 2017, including workshop days). The principles page's metadata shows 11 Aug 2017, apparently a later page date; the principles were released in January 2017, so month precision is used.

events.date_context: January 2017 conference milestone; later web-page metadata is not treated as the original release date.

events.title: Paul Christiano founds the Alignment Research Center (ARC)
events.label: ARC founded
events.problem: Christiano wanted an independent organisation for research on aligning advanced AI systems with human intent.
events.idea: After leaving OpenAI in January 2021, Paul Christiano announced ARC, a non-profit for theoretical 'intent alignment' research (e.g. eliciting latent knowledge).
events.changed: ARC incubated ARC Evals (2022), which ran the pre-release dangerous-capability tests for GPT-4 and Claude and became METR. Its evaluations-plus-thresholds idea fed directly into responsible scaling policies.
events.limits: Its theoretical agenda investigates how explanations and supervision might generalise to much stronger systems. Those methods should not be treated as validated deployment guarantees.

sources.label: Christiano: Announcing the Alignment Research Center (Alignment Forum)

links.note: ARC Evals spun out as METR

terms.def: Eliciting latent knowledge: getting a model to report what it internally 'knows', even when that differs from what it would say to please the evaluator.

verified.note: Alignment Forum lists 26 Apr 2021 (some sources say 27 Apr).

events.title: Anthropic announced by former OpenAI researchers
events.label: Anthropic founded
events.problem: Former OpenAI researchers wanted to investigate the reliability, steerability and interpretability of large-scale models in a new organisation.
events.idea: Dario and Daniela Amodei and colleagues announced Anthropic, a public-benefit corporation, with a $124M Series A to build 'reliable, steerable' AI and study safety at the frontier.
events.changed: Became a major frontier lab and safety-research employer, with work on Constitutional AI, superposition, dictionary learning and alignment science, alongside experiments in corporate governance and responsible scaling.
events.limits: Critics argue a safety-focused lab racing at the frontier still accelerates the race. Its 2026 RSP rewrite and its conflict with the US Department of War show how commercial and political pressure shapes safety commitments.

links.note: founders led GPT-3 and scaling-laws work
Anthropic later published its Responsible Scaling Policy.

terms.def: A for-profit company legally allowed to weigh a stated public mission alongside shareholder returns.

verified.note: Anthropic post dated 28 May 2021. Incorporation was earlier in 2021 (reported Feb 2021, not verified).

events.date_context: Public company/funding announcement, 28 May 2021; this is not an incorporation-date claim.

events.title: Redwood Research founded
events.label: Redwood Research founded
events.problem: Few groups outside the big labs did hands-on empirical alignment work on real language models.
events.idea: Buck Shlegeris, Nate Thomas and Bill Zito founded Redwood Research in Berkeley, first working on adversarial training for high-stakes reliability, then interpretability (causal scrubbing) and running the MLAB / REMIX training programmes.
events.changed: Redwood became the home of 'AI control' (2023): designing protocols that stay safe even if the model is trying to subvert them. Control is now part of lab and government safety cases. It also co-authored the 2024 alignment-faking study with Anthropic.
events.limits: Its early adversarial-training project did not reach its reliability target, which Redwood itself reported. Control assumes trusted monitoring models remain available and may not scale to much stronger systems.

terms.def: Safety measures designed to prevent catastrophe even if the AI system is misaligned and actively trying to evade them.

verified.note: Founding year 2021 agreed across sources; one aggregator gives June 2021, not confirmed by a primary source.

events.date_context: Reported founding year 2021; a dated primary founding announcement was not independently established.

events.title: FLI open letter: 'Pause Giant AI Experiments'
events.label: FLI pause letter
events.problem: GPT-4 (14 March 2023) arrived a few months after ChatGPT; capabilities were moving faster than any oversight process, and labs were racing.
events.idea: FLI's letter called on all labs to pause training of systems more powerful than GPT-4 for at least six months, and to use the time for shared safety protocols and governance. It gathered tens of thousands of signatures, including Bengio, Russell and Musk.
events.changed: A prominent public intervention in the 2023 debate about frontier AI. The CAIS statement, Senate hearings and Bletchley summit followed, but temporal sequence alone does not establish that the letter caused them.
events.limits: The letter did not impose a binding pause or an enforcement mechanism. Signatures and public attention are different from verified changes to training plans.

sources.label: FLI: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter

links.note: the pause threshold was 'more powerful than GPT-4'
second high-profile statement two months later

verified.note: Letter dated 22 March 2023 (FLI history page also places it in March 2023).

events.title: Apollo Research founded to audit models for deception
events.label: Apollo Research founded
events.problem: Independent evaluators were beginning to test frontier models. Apollo proposed a specialised focus on deception and the capabilities that could support it.
events.idea: A starting team led by Marius Hobbhahn announced Apollo Research in London to develop behavioural evaluations and interpretability tools for detecting deceptive alignment. The announcement named researchers and engineers including Lee Sharkey, Lucius Bushnaq, Dan Braun and Mikita Balesni, with Jérémy Scheurer due to join later.
events.changed: Apollo ran pre-deployment scheming evaluations for frontier labs (e.g. OpenAI's o1 in 2024), published evidence of in-context scheming, and co-ran anti-scheming studies with OpenAI (2025). It became a Public Benefit Corporation and opened a San Francisco office in 2026.
events.limits: Behavioural evals can only show that a capability exists, not that it is absent; models that detect evaluation settings make results harder to interpret.

links.note: The organisation later tested o1 before its 2024 deployment; this occurred after the 2023 founding milestone.

terms.def: An AI pursuing hidden, misaligned goals while appearing cooperative, e.g. behaving well during evaluation only.

verified.note: Opened the primary Alignment Forum announcement: 30 May 2023. It identifies starting members and roles, not all of them as co-founders. Current Apollo About page confirms PBC status and San Francisco office in its 2026 timeline.

events.title: CAIS Statement on AI Risk
events.label: CAIS extinction statement
events.problem: The organisers sought a short public statement about catastrophic AI risk that people with different technical and policy views could endorse.
events.idea: The Center for AI Safety published a one-sentence statement saying that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Signers included Hinton, Bengio, Altman, Hassabis and Amodei.
events.changed: Made a concise catastrophic-risk position publicly attributable to prominent scientists and lab leaders. It formed part of the public debate preceding the Bletchley summit; the statement alone does not identify what caused subsequent government decisions.
events.limits: It said nothing about what to do. Critics argued it distracted from present harms, and that CEOs signing while racing ahead was inconsistent.

links.note: The statement preceded the summit; this is a contextual connection, not an independently established causal effect.

verified.note: Released 30 May 2023 (CAIS About says May 2023).

events.title: OpenAI launches the Superalignment team
events.label: Superalignment team launched
events.problem: Humans may be unable to reliably judge future systems' work on difficult tasks. OpenAI proposed research beyond direct human supervision for aligning substantially stronger models.
events.idea: OpenAI created a team co-led by Ilya Sutskever and Jan Leike, promising 20% of its secured compute over four years, to solve superintelligence alignment, with a plan to build a roughly human-level 'automated alignment researcher'.
events.changed: It produced the weak-to-strong generalisation paper and a $10M fast-grants programme, and made 'automated alignment research' a named goal that Anthropic and others later adopted.
events.limits: The team lost both leaders and was dissolved within ten months; Leike said it struggled for compute. The 20% pledge was never publicly verified.

terms.def: Using AI systems themselves to do much of the research needed to align more capable AI systems.

verified.note: Opened the dated OpenAI primary announcement on 6 Nov 2026; confirms 2023-07-05.

events.title: White House voluntary AI commitments
events.label: White House voluntary commitments
events.problem: The US administration sought commitments that companies could adopt quickly while wider AI legislation and standards were still being debated.
events.idea: Seven companies (Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Inflection, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI) committed to pre-release internal and external security testing, information sharing, watermarking research and reporting capabilities and limitations. Eight more joined in September 2023.
events.changed: An early coordinated set of company commitments on testing and disclosure, followed by EO 14110 and later international safety commitments.
events.limits: Voluntary commitments do not provide the enforcement powers of legislation. Their implementation and continuity depend on company conduct and government policy; signing alone is not evidence of compliance.

sources.label: White House fact sheet (21 Jul 2023), archived

links.note: policy response to the ChatGPT moment

verified.note: Archived fact sheet dated 21 July 2023.

events.title: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy
events.label: Anthropic RSP
events.problem: Anthropic wanted a public framework linking increasing model capabilities to stronger security and deployment safeguards.
events.idea: Anthropic defined AI Safety Levels (ASL-1 to ASL-4+, modelled on biosafety levels): capability thresholds checked by evaluations that trigger required security and deployment safeguards, with an implied pause if safeguards are not ready. The idea came from ARC Evals' 'responsible scaling' proposal.
events.changed: Published a concrete conditional framework linking model capabilities to safeguards. OpenAI and Google DeepMind subsequently introduced related frameworks, while Seoul commitments and later transparency laws encouraged public risk-management policies.
events.limits: Self-written and self-enforced; thresholds were vague and could be redefined. Anthropic's own 2026 rewrite (v3) said thresholds proved more ambiguous than expected and dropped the hard commitment to pause, which critics called a weakening.

sources.label: Anthropic: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (19 Sep 2023)

links.note: ARC Evals developed the responsible-scaling concept

terms.def: AI Safety Level: Anthropic's tiered set of required safeguards matched to the dangerous capabilities a model shows.

verified.note: Anthropic post dated 19 Sep 2023.

events.title: US Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure and Trustworthy AI
events.label: US EO 14110
events.problem: The administration sought formal reporting about powerful model development and security testing, alongside government work on evaluation standards.
events.idea: President Biden's order used the Defense Production Act to require developers of models above a compute threshold (10^26 operations) to report training runs and red-team results to the government, and directed NIST to build evaluation standards (leading to the US AI Safety Institute).
events.changed: Used training-compute thresholds as one trigger for federal reporting about powerful models. The EU AI Act and later state proposals used related threshold-based approaches under different legal regimes.
events.limits: An executive order, not a law: it was revoked on 20 January 2025. Reporting requirements were light and enforcement untested.

links.note: turned some voluntary commitments into reporting duties

terms.def: A rule that applies obligations to models trained with more than a set amount of computation, used as a rough proxy for capability.

verified.note: Signed 30 Oct 2023; Federal Register publication 1 Nov 2023.

events.title: AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park and the Bletchley Declaration
events.label: Bletchley AI Safety Summit
events.problem: Governments wanted a dedicated forum for risks from frontier AI, including catastrophic risks, and a shared international statement.
events.idea: The UK hosted 28 countries plus the EU on 1–2 November 2023. They signed the Bletchley Declaration recognising potentially catastrophic risks from frontier AI, and agreed to a state-of-the-science report chaired by Yoshua Bengio. Labs agreed to pre-deployment testing with governments.
events.changed: Began a continuing summit series and commissioned the International AI Safety Report. It also supported the development of government evaluation institutes and international cooperation on frontier-model testing.
events.limits: The declaration was non-binding. Later summits shifted toward 'action', 'impact' and economic opportunity, and the safety focus weakened.

links.note: the summit followed the spring 2023 statements
UK AISI launched at the summit

verified.note: Declaration page title gives 1–2 Nov 2023.

events.title: UK launches the AI Safety Institute
events.label: UK AI Safety Institute
events.problem: Governments wanted their own technical capability to evaluate frontier models rather than relying entirely on developer assessments.
events.idea: The UK turned its Frontier AI Taskforce (set up in 2023 under Ian Hogarth) into the AI Safety Institute, a state body that evaluates frontier models before and after release, staffed with ML researchers recruited from labs. The US announced its own AISI within NIST the same week.
events.changed: Established a prominent government programme for technical frontier-model evaluations, later including the open-source Inspect framework and research on safeguards, alignment and control. It was renamed the AI Security Institute in February 2025.
events.limits: Access to models depends on voluntary lab cooperation; it has no power to block a release.

sources.label: GOV.UK: Prime Minister launches new AI Safety Institute

verified.note: GOV.UK launch release dated 2 Nov 2023 (announcement page resolves).

events.title: OpenAI board fires and then reinstates Sam Altman
events.label: OpenAI board crisis
events.problem: OpenAI's non-profit board was meant to be able to overrule commercial interests for safety, but the mechanism had never been tested.
events.idea: On 17 Nov 2023 the board (including Ilya Sutskever, Helen Toner and Tasha McCauley) removed Altman, saying he had not been consistently candid. After nearly all staff threatened to leave for Microsoft, Altman returned within days and most of the board was replaced.
events.changed: Revealed practical constraints on the non-profit board's authority when staff and commercial partners opposed its decision. The episode became a case study in the difference between formal control and the ability to exercise it.
events.limits: The board's full reasons were never fully public; an outside law-firm review commissioned afterwards did not find grounds requiring removal. Interpretations remain contested.

sources.label: OpenAI: OpenAI announces leadership transition (17 Nov 2023)

verified.note: Opened the dated OpenAI primary announcement on 6 Nov 2026; confirms 2023-11-17.

events.date_context: Removal announcement, 17 November 2023; Altman's return and board changes occurred over the following days.

events.title: ARC Evals spins out as METR
events.label: ARC Evals becomes METR
events.problem: Frontier labs were starting to need independent dangerous-capability testing, but the main evaluator was a project inside a theory non-profit.
events.idea: ARC Evals, started in 2022 by Beth Barnes inside ARC, became an independent non-profit, METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research).
events.changed: METR evaluates autonomy and AI R&D capabilities for major labs, and its 'time horizon' measurements of how long a task agents can complete became a widely cited trend line. It does not take money from AI companies.
events.limits: Evaluations depend on what access labs grant and on elicitation quality; METR itself warns that results are lower bounds on capability.

sources.label: METR: ARC Evals is now METR (4 Dec 2023)

links.note: ARC Evals ran GPT-4 pre-release autonomy tests

terms.def: A test designed to find out whether a model can do something harmful, such as self-replication or cyber offence, before it is deployed.

verified.note: METR blog URL date 4 Dec 2023.

events.title: OpenAI Preparedness Framework (beta)
events.label: OpenAI Preparedness Framework
events.problem: OpenAI had no published rule for when catastrophic-risk capabilities should block deployment.
events.idea: OpenAI published a beta framework that scores models Low/Medium/High/Critical in cybersecurity, CBRN, persuasion and model autonomy; only models at 'Medium' or below post-mitigation can be deployed.
events.changed: OpenAI's analogue of the RSP. Version 2 (15 April 2025) narrowed tracked categories to bio/chem, cyber and AI self-improvement and dropped persuasion.
events.limits: An internal, revisable framework. The 2025 revision says OpenAI may adjust requirements after a competitor releases a high-risk system, subject to publicly acknowledging the change and assessing its risk implications.

sources.label: OpenAI: Our updated Preparedness Framework (15 Apr 2025)

verified.note: Beta date (18 Dec 2023) and v2 date (15 Apr 2025) from search results; beta PDF resolves, openai.com blog returns 403 to automated fetch. The v2 'competitor adjustment' clause is from press coverage, not re-read in the PDF. Reopened15 Apr2025 primary update on 6 Nov2026: confirms tracked categories and the conditional competitor-adjustment clause. Beta-day check remains unresolved.

events.date_context: Beta framework reported on 18 December 2023; the revised framework was announced on 15 April 2025.

events.title: EU AI Act adopted
events.label: EU AI Act
events.problem: The EU sought a broad AI-specific framework with different duties for different risks, including provisions for general-purpose models.
events.idea: The European Parliament adopted the AI Act on 13 March 2024 (Council approval 21 May; entry into force 1 Aug 2024). It is a risk-tiered law: banned practices, high-risk systems, transparency duties, and a late-added chapter on general-purpose AI models, with extra duties for models with 'systemic risk' (presumed above 10^25 training FLOP).
events.changed: Established a broad binding EU framework covering prohibited practices, high-risk systems and general-purpose models. GPAI and systemic-risk provisions include duties concerning documentation, evaluation, risk management and incident reporting, with phased application and enforcement.
events.limits: Application and enforcement were phased, with details developed through standards, guidance and codes. The 2026 AI Omnibus later changed high-risk deadlines; having legal duties is distinct from demonstrating effective compliance.

links.note: Code of Practice implements GPAI duties

terms.def: Under the EU AI Act, a general-purpose model with high-impact capabilities (presumed above 10^25 training FLOP) that carries extra evaluation and reporting duties.

verified.note: Plenary vote 13 Mar 2024 and later dates are well established; europarl.europa.eu returned 403 to curl and EUR-Lex returned 202 (bot check), so URLs were not opened directly. 6 Nov refresh again returned a JavaScript bot check on the Parliament source. Exact vote date remains secondary-verified; the later Commission timeline confirms the legal sequence.

events.date_context: European Parliament vote reported on 13 March 2024; the dated Parliament page could not be read in this check. Council approval and entry into force followed later.

events.title: Future of Humanity Institute closes
events.label: FHI closes
events.problem: FHI had been under an Oxford Faculty of Philosophy hiring and fundraising freeze since 2020.
events.idea: The university closed FHI on 16 April 2024 after 19 years.
events.changed: Closed an influential academic centre for long-term risk research. Its research questions and alumni continued across academic groups, nonprofits, labs and government; the closure did not end philosophical work on these issues.
events.limits: Exact reasons are disputed; FHI's final report blames administrative conflict, and Bostrom had faced controversy over an old email in 2023.

verified.note: Closure date quoted on FHI site.

events.title: OpenAI's Superalignment team dissolved; Jan Leike resigns
events.label: Superalignment dissolved
events.problem: The superalignment team depended on leadership support and compute that, by spring 2024, were in doubt.
events.idea: Ilya Sutskever announced his departure on 14 May 2024; Jan Leike resigned and on 17 May wrote that safety culture had 'taken a backseat to shiny products'. OpenAI confirmed it was folding the team into other groups.
events.changed: A prominent example of safety-team leadership leaving a frontier lab: Leike joined Anthropic and Sutskever co-founded Safe Superintelligence. It contributed to public debate about safety governance and employee protections.
events.limits: OpenAI says safety work continued elsewhere in the company; how much compute the team actually received is not public.

sources.label: CNN: OpenAI exec exits over safety concerns (17 May 2024)

links.note: end of the team launched in 2023
SB 53 later included employee protections; this link does not establish that one team dissolution caused the law.

verified.note: Dates from CNN/Fortune/TechCrunch coverage (17 May 2024). Leike's X thread is the primary source but was not opened.

events.date_context: Public reporting of the team dissolution on 17 May 2024; no dated primary closure announcement was independently checked.

events.title: Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework
events.label: DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework
events.problem: Google DeepMind had safety teams but no public threshold-based policy like Anthropic's RSP.
events.idea: Anca Dragan, Helen King and Allan Dafoe introduced Critical Capability Levels in autonomy, biosecurity, cybersecurity and ML R&D, checked by early-warning evaluations that trigger security and deployment mitigations.
events.changed: Added Google DeepMind's published capability-threshold framework to those already released by Anthropic and OpenAI before the Seoul summit. It made the lab's proposed risk categories and mitigation process available for public comparison.
events.limits: Described by Google itself as exploratory; commitments are internal and revisable, without outside enforcement.

sources.label: Google DeepMind: Introducing the Frontier Safety Framework (17 May 2024)

terms.def: Google DeepMind's threshold at which a model's capability in a risk domain requires specific mitigations.

verified.note: Post dated 17 May 2024. Later versions (v2 early 2025, v3 Sept 2025) are mentioned from memory and not re-verified.

events.title: AI Seoul Summit and Frontier AI Safety Commitments
events.label: Seoul AI Summit
events.problem: Governments sought wider company commitments to publish risk thresholds, safeguards and procedures for severe frontier-AI risks.
events.idea: Co-hosted by South Korea and the UK on 21–22 May 2024. Sixteen companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, xAI, Mistral and Zhipu AI, pledged to publish safety frameworks with risk thresholds and, in extreme cases, not to develop or deploy a model if risks could not be kept below them. Countries launched an international network of AI safety institutes.
events.changed: Turned the RSP idea into a cross-industry norm; by 2025, 12 companies had published frameworks (per the 2026 International AI Safety Report).
events.limits: The commitments are voluntary. Publishing a framework does not by itself establish the quality of evaluations or that a company will follow it under pressure.

sources.label: GOV.UK: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024

verified.note: Commitments page resolves; summit dates 21–22 May 2024 are standard and consistent with the page.

events.title: California Governor vetoes SB 1047
events.label: SB 1047 vetoed
events.problem: No US law placed safety duties on developers of the largest models.
events.idea: SB 1047 (Senator Scott Wiener) would have required developers of very large models to adopt safety protocols, be able to shut models down, and take reasonable care against critical harms, with liability. It passed the legislature but Gov. Newsom vetoed it, arguing it targeted model size rather than risky use.
events.changed: The fight split the AI industry (Anthropic cautiously supported the final version; OpenAI, Meta and many investors opposed it) and became the template for the narrower SB 53.
events.limits: The veto left no US frontier-safety statute in 2024; critics say the size-based approach was crude, supporters say liability was the point.

verified.note: Veto message PDF resolves; veto dated 29 Sep 2024.

events.title: Trump revokes Executive Order 14110
events.label: EO 14110 revoked
events.problem: The incoming administration saw Biden's AI order as a barrier to innovation.
events.idea: On his first day, President Trump revoked EO 14110 (via EO 14148, 'Initial Rescissions'), and on 23 Jan 2025 issued EO 14179 calling for an AI Action Plan focused on US dominance.
events.changed: Ended the US reporting regime for frontier training runs and shifted federal policy from 'safety' to 'security and innovation', which led to the CAISI rename and the July 2025 AI Action Plan.
events.limits: Some evaluation work survived in NIST/CAISI and in voluntary lab agreements.

sources.label: Federal Register: Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions (EO 14148)

links.note: policy shift behind the CAISI rename

verified.note: Federal Register document resolves (signed 20 Jan 2025, published 28 Jan 2025).

events.title: First International AI Safety Report
events.label: International AI Safety Report
events.problem: Governments lacked a shared, independent summary of evidence on what general-purpose AI can do and how risky it is, the way the IPCC serves climate policy.
events.idea: Commissioned at Bletchley and chaired by Yoshua Bengio, about 100 experts nominated by 30 countries plus the UN, OECD and EU summarised evidence on capabilities, risks (malicious use, malfunction, systemic) and mitigations, ahead of the Paris summit.
events.changed: Became the reference document for policymakers; a second edition followed in Feb 2026 and interim 'key updates' in between.
events.limits: It deliberately makes no policy recommendations, and it reports deep expert disagreement on timelines and loss-of-control risk rather than resolving it.

sources.label: arXiv: International AI Safety Report (v1 29 Jan 2025)

verified.note: arXiv v1 29 Jan 2025 (API checked). The old gov.uk publication URL now redirects to internationalaisafetyreport.org. Reopened arXiv abstract/submission-history pages on 6 Nov 2026: 2501.17805.

events.date_context: Report publication/arXiv v1, 29 January 2025; later interim updates are separate publications.

events.title: AI Action Summit in Paris
events.label: Paris AI Action Summit
events.problem: The summit series had to decide whether to stay focused on frontier safety or broaden to adoption and economics.
events.idea: France and India co-chaired the summit on 10–11 Feb 2025. The final statement on 'inclusive and sustainable' AI was signed by about 60 countries including China, but not the US or UK. US Vice President Vance criticised 'excessive regulation'.
events.changed: Marked a clear shift in the summit series away from safety; the UK renamed its institute to 'Security' days later.
events.limits: Safety advocates called it a missed opportunity; others say broadening was needed to keep developing countries involved.

sources.label: Élysée: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable AI (11 Feb 2025)

verified.note: Élysée statement page resolves (11 Feb 2025). Signatory count varies by source (58–61).

events.title: UK AI Safety Institute becomes AI Security Institute; US AISI becomes CAISI
events.label: Safety institutes rebranded
events.problem: UK and US governments reframed their evaluation institutions around security, standards and innovation, while retaining technical testing functions.
events.idea: On 14 Feb 2025 the UK renamed its institute the AI Security Institute, focusing on national-security and crime risks (bio/chem, cyber, fraud, CSAM) and saying it would not focus on bias or free speech. On 3 Jun 2025 the US Commerce Secretary turned the US AI Safety Institute into the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at NIST, focused on voluntary standards, national-security evaluations and competition with foreign models.
events.changed: Both bodies kept doing technical evaluations; the UK one kept and expanded alignment and control research. The rename signalled a political reframing of the same work from 'safety' to 'security'.
events.limits: Names and priorities can change without ending the underlying evaluation work. The current NIST page uses CAISSI; its further rename date was not established, so this card remains anchored to the 2025 changes.

sources.label: GOV.UK: Tackling AI security risks (14 Feb 2025)
US Commerce: Lutnick statement on transforming the US AISI (3 Jun 2025)

verified.note: UK page read (14 Feb 2025). US date 3 Jun 2025 confirmed by several outlets; commerce.gov returns 403 to automated fetch.

events.date_context: UK rename on 14 February 2025; the US CAISI rename followed in June. The current NIST page uses CAISSI without a verified rename date.

events.title: EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice; GPAI obligations apply (2 Aug 2025)
events.label: EU GPAI Code of Practice
events.problem: The AI Act's GPAI duties were abstract; providers needed a concrete way to show compliance.
events.idea: Independent experts drafted, and the Commission published on 10 July 2025, a voluntary Code with three chapters: transparency, copyright, and safety & security (for systemic-risk models, effectively requiring a frontier safety framework, evaluations and incident reporting). GPAI obligations began applying on 2 Aug 2025.
events.changed: Most frontier labs signed (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Mistral, Amazon; xAI only the safety chapter). It turned RSP-style practice into an EU compliance route.
events.limits: Meta refused to sign. The Commission's enforcement powers over GPAI start only from Aug 2026, so early compliance is largely self-reported.

sources.label: European Commission: Contents of the GPAI Code of Practice

verified.note: Commission page confirms 10 July 2025 publication and signatory list. 2 Aug 2025 application date is from the Act's timeline (not on that page). Meta's refusal is press-reported.

events.date_context: Code publication on 10 July 2025; GPAI obligations began applying on 2 August 2025.

events.title: California SB 53, Transparency in Frontier AI Act, signed
events.label: California SB 53
events.problem: After the SB 1047 veto there was still no US law on frontier-model safety.
events.idea: Newsom signed Senator Wiener's narrower bill: large frontier developers must publish a safety framework and transparency reports at release, report critical safety incidents to the state within 15 days, and protect whistleblowers; it also starts a public compute consortium (CalCompute). In force 1 Jan 2026.
events.changed: Made publication of frontier safety frameworks and other transparency measures statutory requirements in California. It is a concrete example of public law building on practices that developers had previously set voluntarily.
events.limits: Mostly disclosure: no mandatory third-party audits or shutdown capability; enforcement is by civil penalty. A federal preemption push could limit state laws.

sources.label: Governor of California: Newsom signs SB 53 (29 Sep 2025)

verified.note: Opened Governor of California primary signing announcement dated 29 Sep 2025. Legal details should be read with the enacted statute; this flag confirms the signing milestone.

events.title: OpenAI recapitalisation into Foundation + Public Benefit Corporation
events.label: OpenAI recapitalisation
events.problem: OpenAI's capped-profit structure under a non-profit made raising capital hard, and its 2024–25 plan to drop non-profit control met legal and public opposition.
events.idea: OpenAI completed a restructuring in which the non-profit OpenAI Foundation retained control of the for-profit OpenAI Group PBC. The arrangement combines a public-benefit corporate form with non-profit governance and an equity stake in the business.
events.changed: Retained formal non-profit control in a new corporate structure, leaving practical oversight an ongoing question. In September 2026 Paul Christiano joined the Foundation board and its Safety and Security Committee.
events.limits: Critics argue non-profit control is weaker in practice once most value sits with investors; state attorneys general negotiated conditions.

sources.label: TechCrunch: OpenAI completes its for-profit recapitalization (28 Oct 2025)
Paul Christiano joins Foundation board (9 September 2026)

verified.note: Opened OpenAI primary announcements: recapitalisation completed 28 Oct 2025; Christiano appointment 9 Sep 2026. Public wording no longer depends on secondary equity estimates or a claim that governance was settled.

events.date_context: Completed restructuring announced 28 October 2025; Christiano's board appointment was a later September 2026 event.

events.title: International AI Safety Report 2026 (second edition)
events.label: AI Safety Report 2026
events.problem: One year on, capabilities (reasoning models, agents) and evidence of risks had moved fast.
events.idea: Bengio's panel, over 100 experts backed by 30+ countries and organisations, reported jagged but rapid capability gains (IMO gold-level maths, multi-hour agentic coding), growing real-world evidence of misuse, models that can tell tests from deployment, and that 12 companies had published or updated frontier safety frameworks in 2025.
events.changed: Supplied the evidence base for the New Delhi summit and flagged evaluation awareness as a problem for safety testing.
events.limits: Still no recommendations; it found most risk management remains voluntary and that safeguards have significant limits.

links.note: Published 3 February 2026, before the February summit; the summit card uses month precision, not a 1 February date.

verified.note: Official page gives 3 Feb 2026; Bengio's site lists 6 Feb; arXiv v1 is 24 Feb 2026. Reopened arXiv abstract/submission-history pages on 6 Nov 2026: 2602.21012.

events.date_context: Official report publication, 3 February 2026; arXiv v1 appeared later, on 24 February.

events.title: India AI Impact Summit and New Delhi Declaration
events.label: New Delhi AI Impact Summit
events.problem: The summit series continued in India with a broad AI-impact agenda, including international cooperation and access.
events.idea: India hosted the AI Impact Summit in February 2026 and announced the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact. Public accounts also describe company commitments, but their detailed content and complete signatory lists are not independently established in this record.
events.changed: Continued the international summit series with greater emphasis on AI's economic and social impact. A common declaration is a cooperation milestone rather than evidence that national policies or evaluation capacity have converged.
events.limits: Participation and endorsement do not establish implementation. Exact event-day ranges and counts vary with the sessions and signatories being counted, so the timeline uses month precision.

sources.label: Government of India (NeGD): AI Impact Summit 2026 concludes with New Delhi Declaration
ThePrint: 88 nations adopt New Delhi Declaration

verified.note: Opened NeGD primary page: identifies February 2026 and gives 18–19 Feb for the summit; broader-event dates differ across accounts. Month-level anchor is verified, exact day range not asserted.

events.date_context: February 2026 summit; public accounts differ on main-session versus wider-event dates, so month precision is retained.

events.title: Anthropic RSP v3: unilateral commitments separated from industry-wide map
events.label: Anthropic RSP v3
events.problem: Anthropic found its if-then thresholds 'far more ambiguous' than expected, and higher safeguard levels (e.g. top-tier weight security) possibly impossible for one company alone.
events.idea: RSP v3 separates what Anthropic will do regardless of others from a recommended industry-wide map of capabilities to mitigations; it adds a public Frontier Safety Roadmap and Risk Reports every 3–6 months, with external review in some cases.
events.changed: Changed the structure of Anthropic's policy toward explicit unilateral commitments, an industry-wide capability-to-mitigation map, and more public reporting. This makes the content and strength of particular commitments important to compare across policy versions.
events.limits: A public roadmap and risk reports do not provide the same assurance as enforceable safeguards. Whether the revision improves accountability or weakens restraint depends on its specific commitments and implementation.

sources.label: Anthropic: Responsible Scaling Policy v3 (24 Feb 2026)

links.note: Risk Reports and frameworks now also serve legal transparency duties

verified.note: Anthropic page read (24 Feb 2026). Point-release dates from search summaries only.

events.title: Pentagon designates Anthropic a 'supply chain risk'
events.label: Anthropic–Pentagon dispute
events.problem: Anthropic's restrictions on military uses came into conflict with a government customer's demands, testing the practical force of developer use policies.
events.idea: After Anthropic maintained restrictions on mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, the President announced that federal agencies should stop using its models and Hegseth announced a supply-chain-risk designation. Anthropic says it received written notice on 4 March 2026. The designation and related government actions led to litigation.
events.changed: Made the conflict between a lab's use restrictions and a government customer's demands concrete. It illustrates that state procurement and security powers can exert pressure on developer policies.
events.limits: Anthropic contests the designation's legality and scope. September press reports describe different outcomes in D.C. and California proceedings; this card does not independently certify those court holdings or a final legal outcome.

sources.label: Washington Times: Pentagon designates Anthropic supply chain risk (27 Feb 2026)
CP24/AP: Federal court says Pentagon can label Anthropic a supply chain risk (25 Sep 2026)
Anthropic: written notice received 4 March (statement 5 March)

verified.note: The 5 Mar 2026 company statement explicitly says written notice was received on 4 Mar. The Feb 27 public announcements are linked by that statement; court outcomes remain secondary-only and are not stated as settled facts.

events.date_context: Public designation announcement, 27 February 2026; written notice was received 4 March and confirmed publicly 5 March.

events.title: EU Digital Omnibus on AI: political agreement delays high-risk rules
events.label: EU AI Omnibus deal
events.problem: Industry and member states said high-risk AI Act obligations due 2 Aug 2026 were unworkable without finished standards.
events.idea: EU institutions reached a political agreement on 7 May 2026 to amend the AI Act's implementation timetable, including later dates for high-risk requirements and a ban on certain non-consensual sexual-image systems. Parliament adopted its position on 16 June, Council acted on 29 June, and the amendment entered into force on 27 July 2026.
events.changed: Changed high-risk implementation dates to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for product-related systems. It demonstrates that implementation timetables can be revised after a law is adopted.
events.limits: The amendment changes selected obligations and deadlines rather than replacing the AI Act. Effects on compliance and enforcement depend on later implementation; delay alone does not measure safety outcomes.

sources.label: Sidley Data Matters: provisional agreement to delay AI Act obligations
techUK: EU AI Omnibus deal reached (7 May 2026)
Commission: AI Omnibus enters into force (27 July 2026)

verified.note: Commission primary pages confirm political agreement 7 May and entry into force 27 July 2026. Parliament Legislative Observatory identifies Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Parliament position 16 June and Council decision 29 June. Original agreement date retained as the milestone.

events.date_context: Political agreement, 7 May 2026; final amendment entered into force on 27 July 2026.

events.title: US EO 14409: voluntary pre-release access for frontier models (cyber focus)
events.label: US EO 14409
events.problem: Frontier-model cyber capabilities raised national-security concerns, while the administration sought cooperation with industry without a licensing regime.
events.idea: The order creates a classified cyber-capability benchmark run by Treasury, NSA and CISA; the NSA Director designates 'covered frontier models'; developers may voluntarily give the government up to 30 days of pre-release access and coordinate trusted early access for critical-infrastructure partners. It states it creates no licensing or preclearance requirement.
events.changed: Added a voluntary, cyber-focused process for government access and coordination around covered frontier models. This differs from EO 14110's earlier reporting requirements.
events.limits: Voluntary; no safety testing mandate and no power to block release.

sources.label: White House: Promoting Advanced AI Innovation and Security (2 Jun 2026)

verified.note: White House page read: signed 2 Jun 2026, EO number 14409. The Mythos link is from secondary coverage.

events.title: CHERI becomes Pivotal Research; fellowship moves to London
events.label: Pivotal Research (ex-CHERI)
events.problem: CHERI sought to support new researchers through mentored projects and a shared research environment; the 2024 programme moved that fellowship activity to London.
events.idea: The Swiss Existential Risk Initiative (CHERI), which had run summer research fellowships since 2021, renamed itself Pivotal Research and ran its fourth fellowship (9 weeks, 1 Jul–30 Aug 2024) at the LISA offices in London, alongside groups such as Apollo Research, BlueDot and the MATS extension.
events.changed: Developed into a longer mentor-led fellowship covering technical AI safety, governance and biosecurity. Its public page schedules a 15-week AI Safety Fellowship for 18 January–30 April 2027 at LISA in London.
events.limits: Fellowships produce mostly short projects; impact depends on mentor quality and on fellows finding jobs afterwards.

sources.label: LessWrong: Apply to the Pivotal Research Fellowship (10 Apr 2024)

links.note: CHERI fellowship was funded by Open Philanthropy grants (2023)

verified.note: Rename post dated 10 Apr 2024. CHERI start year 2021 inferred from '4th fellowship' in 2024 and alumni labelled 2021 on pivotal-research.org/about.

events.date_context: CHERI-to-Pivotal rename announcement, 10 April 2024; the fellowship predecessor operated earlier.

orgs.name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI; SIAI until 2013)
orgs.historical_role: An early independent home for Friendly AI and agent-foundations research, including corrigibility and decision theory; its community contributed to later alignment work.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Its public agenda emphasises technical governance, communication and policy advocating restraint on frontier development, alongside its historical technical-alignment work.

orgs.name: Future of Humanity Institute (Oxford)
orgs.historical_role: An influential academic home for existential-risk, macrostrategy and AI-governance work; Bostrom wrote Superintelligence there, and GovAI originated as an FHI programme.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Closed on 16 April 2024; the archival website and final report remain sources for its research and institutional history.

orgs.name: DeepMind / Google DeepMind
orgs.historical_role: An AGI-focused lab that produced DQN and AlphaGo; acquired by Google in 2014 and merged with Google Brain in 2023. Research includes alignment, evaluations and interpretability.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Google DeepMind publishes alignment and interpretability research and a Frontier Safety Framework. Formal frameworks and research outputs are evidence to inspect, rather than guarantees of safety.

orgs.name: Future of Life Institute
orgs.historical_role: Bridged AI-risk concerns to mainstream researchers (Puerto Rico 2015, Asilomar 2017) and to the public (2023 pause letter); funded early safety grants.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Works on AI policy, advocacy, grantmaking and evaluation of frontier developers through its AI Safety Index.

orgs.name: OpenAI
orgs.historical_role: A major frontier lab behind GPT models, scaled RLHF and ChatGPT. Its corporate governance and safety-team history provide cases for analysing mission and commercial incentives.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: OpenAI Group PBC is controlled by the OpenAI Foundation following the October 2025 recapitalisation. Christiano joined the Foundation board and Safety and Security Committee in September 2026.

orgs.name: Open Philanthropy (renamed Coefficient Giving, Nov 2025)
orgs.historical_role: A major funder of AI-safety institutions, technical research, governance and researcher training since prioritising advanced-AI risk in 2016.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Renamed Coefficient Giving on 18 November 2025; its multi-donor philanthropic work includes advanced-AI risk and biosecurity.

sources.label: Coefficient Giving: The story behind our new name

orgs.name: Center for Human-Compatible AI (UC Berkeley)
orgs.historical_role: An academic centre that developed assistance-game and preference-learning approaches to beneficial AI and trained researchers who later worked across the field.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: A multi-institution academic group based at UC Berkeley, researching provably beneficial AI and systems that learn human preferences.

orgs.name: EleutherAI
orgs.historical_role: Open models, datasets and training-analysis tools such as GPT-Neo/NeoX, the Pile and Pythia expanded access to language-model research outside large commercial labs.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: An independent nonprofit producing open models, datasets and tools for understanding training and model behaviour.

orgs.name: Anthropic
orgs.historical_role: A frontier lab founded by former OpenAI researchers, with contributions to Constitutional AI, interpretability and alignment science and an influential responsible-scaling policy.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Publishes Claude models, alignment-science and interpretability research, and responsible-scaling policies. Its February 2026 RSP v3 changed the structure of its public commitments.

orgs.name: Alignment Research Center (ARC)
orgs.historical_role: A theoretical alignment organisation that incubated ARC Evals, which became METR; its research includes eliciting latent knowledge and mechanistic estimation.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Active in theoretical alignment research: its website lists May and June 2026 work on mechanistic estimation and a White-Box Estimation Challenge.

orgs.name: Redwood Research
orgs.historical_role: Empirical alignment lab that created the 'AI control' agenda and co-authored the alignment-faking study.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Active in AI control, strategic-deception research and applied advice on misalignment risks; its public work includes control safety cases with UK AISI.

orgs.name: MATS (ML Alignment & Theory Scholars; began as SERI MATS)
founders: SERI MATS founding team (individual founders not established here)
orgs.historical_role: A research-mentorship programme connecting new researchers with alignment, interpretability and security mentors; alumni have joined or founded research organisations.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Runs 12-week research fellowships in Berkeley and London, with an application-based 6–12 month extension. The public programme spans alignment, transparency and security.

orgs.name: Conjecture
orgs.historical_role: A London alignment company founded by EleutherAI alumni; pursued Cognitive Emulation, interpretability and policy advocacy.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Its website presents a Cognitive Emulation agenda. ControlAI identifies founder Connor Leahy as its US Executive Director; Conjecture's claimed wind-down date and current operations remain unverified.

orgs.name: FAR.AI
orgs.historical_role: Research and field-building non-profit (robustness, adversarial attacks on superhuman Go AIs, deception probes) that runs the Alignment Workshop series and FAR.Labs co-working space.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: An AI-security research and adoption nonprofit, combining foundational and applied work with workshops, grantmaking and engagement with developers and governments.

orgs.name: Center for AI Safety (CAIS)
orgs.historical_role: A research and field-building nonprofit behind the 2023 AI-risk statement, researcher compute support and evaluation work such as WMDP. Its director also co-authored MMLU before CAIS was founded.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: A nonprofit directed by Dan Hendrycks and Oliver Zhang, conducting AI-risk research, evaluations and field-building.

orgs.name: Apollo Research
founders: Marius Hobbhahn (co-founder; starting team documented in 2023 announcement)
orgs.historical_role: Third-party evaluator focused on scheming and deceptive alignment; ran pre-deployment tests for frontier labs.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Now a Public Benefit Corporation, with London and San Francisco offices. Research focuses on scheming evaluations and mitigation; Watcher applies monitoring to frontier agents.

orgs.name: UK AI Safety Institute → AI Security Institute
founders: UK Government (DSIT); built from the Frontier AI Taskforce under Ian Hogarth
orgs.historical_role: A government programme for technical frontier-model evaluations and research on safeguards, alignment and control; an early participant in international institute cooperation.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Operates as the AI Security Institute. Its research covers model evaluations, cyber and biological risks, safeguards, alignment and control.

orgs.name: US AISI → CAISI → CAISSI (NIST)
founders: US Department of Commerce / NIST under EO 14110
orgs.historical_role: US government evaluator created under EO 14110; rebranded in 2025 toward standards, national-security evaluations and assessing foreign models.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: The NIST page formerly at /caisi now redirects to /caissi and uses the name Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI). The rename date was not established; its public remit includes voluntary standards and national-security evaluations.

orgs.name: METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research; ex-ARC Evals)
orgs.historical_role: Pioneered third-party dangerous-capability and autonomy evaluations (GPT-4, Claude) and the time-horizon trend measure; its ideas underpin lab scaling policies.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: An independent nonprofit led by Beth Barnes, studying autonomous capabilities, evaluation methods and unintended agent behaviour. It states that it does not accept funding from AI companies.

orgs.name: Goodfire
orgs.historical_role: Venture-backed interpretability company, a sign that mechanistic interpretability became commercially fundable.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: An interpretability company working on model understanding and interventions; its May 2026 VPD work analysed a small language model's parameter components.

orgs.name: Transluce
orgs.historical_role: Non-profit building open, AI-agent-driven interpretability and behaviour-elicitation tools so that labs are not the only judges of their own models.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: An independent nonprofit developing open tools for understanding model internals and agent behaviour; its current site also presents incident investigations and agent-behaviour analysis tools.

orgs.name: Pivotal Research (ex-Swiss Existential Risk Initiative, CHERI)
founders: Naomi Nederlof (identified by Pivotal as Founder & Advisor)
orgs.historical_role: A London-based research fellowship descended from CHERI, supporting mentored projects in technical AI safety, AI governance and biosecurity.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Runs research fellowships in London. Its public site identifies Pivotal Research Ltd as a UK nonprofit company limited by guarantee, distinct from the earlier CHERI fellowship activity.
orgs.founded_context: CHERI fellowship documented from 2021; Pivotal name announced 2024

orgs.name: Meta FAIR (Fundamental AI Research)
orgs.historical_role: A research lab associated with self-supervised learning and the LLaMA open-weight models. Its approach is relevant to debates about open model access and risk management.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: Meta's July 2025 earnings remarks placed FAIR within Meta Superintelligence Labs. FAIR's public research releases include agents, robustness, safety and model architectures; this record does not assert a current leadership roster.

orgs.historical_role: Bengio's safe-by-design non-profit, building a non-agentic 'Scientist AI' intended to act as a guardrail on AI agents.
orgs.status_as_of_2026_11: A nonprofit launched by Yoshua Bengio in June 2025 to investigate safe-by-design, non-agentic Scientist AI. The proposed safety benefits remain research goals.

threads.title: How did AI safety become an institutional field?
threads.question: How did a mailing-list concern in 2000 become a set of labs, non-profits, funders, fellowships and government institutes by 2026?
threads.summary: Early independent and academic groups such as SIAI/MIRI and FHI developed long-term AI-risk arguments. DeepMind and OpenAI pursued general AI through research labs; FLI, philanthropic funding and CHAI widened the research community, while Concrete Problems in 2016 articulated an empirical agenda. From 2021, organisations including Anthropic, ARC, Redwood, Apollo and METR developed different combinations of alignment research, evaluations and control. Fellowships and government institutes expanded entry routes. The OpenAI board crisis, safety-team departures and revisions to scaling policies illustrate continuing tensions between formal commitments and practical incentives.

threads.title: How did governments start to respond?
threads.question: When and how did states move from ignoring frontier AI risk to testing models and passing laws, and how far did that go?
threads.summary: The selected milestones trace a frontier-risk policy strand, not the beginning of all AI governance. The 2023 company commitments, EO 14110 and Bletchley summit connected model testing with government attention. The EU AI Act and California SB 53 added different legal duties; Seoul promoted public company frameworks. Later US policy revoked EO 14110 and emphasised voluntary, security-focused cooperation, while the EU amended high-risk implementation dates. The Anthropic–Pentagon dispute illustrates a separate issue: government pressure on a developer's use restrictions. These measures differ in legal force, and their existence does not establish effective enforcement or reduced risk.
